guard: `cotal attach` re-establishes its session when the LINK dies, and stops, saying why, when re-establishing cannot help
completionMarker: F. the four classifications the loop turns on
why: SPECIFIER BOUNDARY, and it is the reason every command here builds first. The suite reads the
code under test through TWO different paths on purpose. Cell F imports `attachRefusal`,
`isTransportEnd` and `reconnectNotice` from `implementations/cli/src` directly, so a mutation lands on the bytes it
grades with no build at all. Cells A to E run the real binary, `tsx bin/cotal.ts`, and
`@cotal-ai/cli` resolves to `dist/` -- so those cells audit the last BUILD. Without a build in
the command a mutation would kill the hand-built cell and leave every end-to-end cell green,
which reads as `the classifier matters` when what was actually measured is `the suite imports
the classifier`. Each mutation therefore builds the CLI first and rebuilds it in afterRestore,
because `dist/` is gitignored and git cannot be the recovery for it.
THE PAIRING IS THE POINT, not the count. Cell F builds its inputs by hand, so on its own it
proves only that the suite depends on those three functions. Mutations 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 are
aimed at END-TO-END cells, which is what shows a real entry point reaches them: mutation 4 changes what
`attachRefusal` answers for `not-found` and the despawn cell goes red, having travelled the
whole path from a real `cotal stop` through the manager's reply code into the loop's verdict.
Mutations 3 and 9 are the ones aimed at hand-built cells, and each says why in its own note:
nothing this harness can do makes the manager answer `permission-denied` (a static single-owner
mesh mints an admin instrument for every attach), and nothing here can produce a hand-back that
FAILED on the same attempt whose control ask SUCCEEDED over the same broker.
NOT GRADED, and MEASURED rather than asserted. The loop's own `denied` BRANCH -- the line that
turns a `denied` classification into a non-zero exit rather than another retry -- has no
end-to-end cell, for the reason above. Deleting `est.kind === \"denied\"` from that condition
is a SURVIVOR, and the first attempt to show that was thrown out: run alone it came back
UNGRADABLE, because a suite passing with a mutation applied proves nothing until something
shows the suite reaches that file at runtime at all. Applies and mutates are different
properties. Re-run PAIRED with a positive control in the same file (`not-found` -> `transient`,
which reddens cell E end to end), the control was KILLED and the branch deletion SURVIVED, so
the survivor is a real coverage gap rather than an unexecuted line. What IS proved is the
classification (mutation 3) and the loop's handling of the two classifications this harness CAN
produce, `gone` (mutation 4, cell E) and `transient` (cells A and B). The gap is the mapping
from `denied` to the exit, stated here rather than left for a reader to infer from a kill count.
The pairing is not in this config on purpose: a committed kill set with a deliberate survivor
exits non-zero for everyone who runs it afterwards, which trains readers to ignore the verdict.
MUTATION 1 IS AIMED AT `connection-closed` AND NOT AT `gap`, which is worth saying because
`gap` is the reason the original defect was FOUND. `gap` is what the client saw when the link
healed quickly; the fix stops waiting for that symptom and acts on the connection going away,
so `connection-closed` is the member of the set the end-to-end cells actually travel through.
Aiming at `gap` would have produced a survivor and a false sense of coverage.
MUTATIONS 6 AND 7 GRADE THE TWO THINGS THIS CHANGE ADDED BEYOND THE LOOP ITSELF, and both are
aimed end to end. 6 makes a reconnecting client forget the session it abandoned, and cell H reads
the manager's OWN live-session count to catch it: that cell uses a SILENT seat on purpose, because
a ticking seat fills the send window, arms the rail's stall watchdog and reaps the abandoned
session for free -- which would have made the client's hand-back look load-bearing when it was not.
7 lets a LOCAL refusal reach the terminal, and cell A catches it, because the mesh preflight really
does refuse there for several backoff rungs while the broker is down. Cell F's third check pins the
same branch by hand; the kill at cell A is what shows the real binary travels it.
MUTATIONS 8 AND 9 CAME OUT OF REVIEW, and 8 is worth reading before the others because it grades a
defect the suite had already passed over. The hand-back used to treat a local publish as delivery.
Publishing to NATS is a buffer write; the FLUSH is the round trip that says the frame left. Cell B
detaches while the link is still down, so it is the one cell that reaches the exit with a session
genuinely unhandled, and its line was ABSENT on the buggy code. That absence is how the defect was
found, and mutation 8 is the same absence on demand.
MUTATION 12 GRADES A DEFECT THIS SUITE SHIPPED WITH, found by measuring the cell it was hiding
behind. Cell J asserted a clean exit and got one: the detach was honoured immediately, the
terminal came back, `detached from` printed. What no assertion looked at was WHEN the process
ended. The backoff `sleep` lost its race and was never cleared, so node held the command open to
the end of the rung, up to 30 seconds of a shell that had already said it detached. A limit
measured after the work is no limit, so the assertion is bounded against the next attempt's own
position, which is the only clock the defect is expressed in.

mutations.name: `connection-closed` is dropped from the transport-class set, so the link dying is treated as the session finishing
mutations.expectRed: the link dying is announced on the terminal
mutations.cell: the link dying is announced on the terminal
mutations.note: The defect as shipped, in one list entry. Without this member the attach reads a dead link as a finished session, prints `detached from` and exits, which is the behaviour the whole change exists to remove. It is aimed at the end-to-end cell rather than at cell F deliberately: cell F would redden too, and a kill there alone would not show that the real binary travels this path.

mutations.name: `detached` joins the transport-class set, so pressing the detach key starts a reconnect instead of ending the attach
mutations.expectRed: the detach key still detaches after a reconnect
mutations.cell: the detach key still detaches after a reconnect
mutations.note: The opposite error, and the more dangerous one, because it is invisible until someone tries to leave: an operator who presses Ctrl-] gets `[cotal: connection lost, reconnecting]` and a terminal that will not give itself back. The set has to be wrong in BOTH directions to be worth asserting, so this is the pair to mutation 1.

mutations.name: a manager's `permission-denied` is classified as worth retrying
mutations.note: A manager that has said no does not change its mind, so reading its refusal as transient turns one refusal into an unbounded retry loop against it. This is the mutation aimed at the hand-built cell, and the reason is in `why`: nothing in this harness makes a static single-owner mesh answer `permission-denied`. Its sibling, mutation 4, is what shows the same function is reached from the real binary.

mutations.name: a seat the manager no longer knows is classified as worth retrying
mutations.expectRed: ...clean, saying the seat is gone (not an infinite retry against something that is not there)
mutations.cell: ...clean, saying the seat is gone (not an infinite retry against something that is not there)
mutations.note: THE REACHABILITY PROOF for the classifier. This is one line in a pure function, and the cell it reddens is a full end-to-end run: a real `cotal stop` despawns the seat while the client is reconnecting, the manager answers `not-found` on the wire, the CLI's inspect resolution carries that code, and the loop turns it into a clean exit. A kill here is the evidence that cell F is grading a function the product actually calls, rather than one the suite happens to import.

mutations.name: the first attach takes the RETRY path, so its refusal is rethrown instead of printed and exited
mutations.find: const t = await resolveControlTarget(v, "control-caller-admin", on, first ? {} : { onRefusal: "throw" });
mutations.replace: const t = await resolveControlTarget(v, "control-caller-admin", on, reconnect ? { onRefusal: "throw" } : {});
mutations.expectRed: ...with ONE failure mark, not the doubled one a rethrown refusal renders
mutations.cell: ...with ONE failure mark, not the doubled one a rethrown refusal renders
mutations.note: The shipped defect, restored. `reconnect` is ON by default, so keying the disposition on the flag rather than on `first` sends the very first attach down the path meant only for re-establishments: its refusal escapes as an exception, the dispatcher's generic handler renders it as `✗ ${message}` over a sentence that already opens with `✗`, and the refusal's hint line is dropped. Aimed at the ONE load-bearing check in cell G: non-zero exit, the `no mesh running` sentence, and the absent reconnect banner all stay green under this mutation, because a first-attempt connect failure never announces a reconnect on either path. A kill here is therefore a claim about the failure MARK specifically, which is the whole finding.

mutations.name: a reconnecting client forgets the session it abandoned, so it never hands it back
mutations.find: abandoned.push({ grant: est.grant, creds: est.creds, inbox: est.inbox, server: est.server });
mutations.expectRed: ...and the reconnect left ONE live session, not two: the abandoned one was handed back
mutations.cell: ...and the reconnect left ONE live session, not two: the abandoned one was handed back
mutations.note: The state of the world before this change, restored in one word. When the link is gone the client is the only party that knows the session is over -- nothing on the serving side reaps a session whose caller went away while the seat is quiet -- so a client that does not record the abandoned session's credential can never tell the manager, and each outage costs one of its 64 slots. Aimed at cell H, which is end to end: a real seat, a real severed link, a real re-establishment, and the manager's own live-session count read on the way through.

mutations.name: a LOCAL refusal is relayed to the terminal, so a dropped wifi is answered with `run `cotal up``
mutations.expectRed: a broker that is down AT the reconnect step produces another wait, never an exit
mutations.cell: a broker that is down AT the reconnect step produces another wait, never an exit
mutations.note: The notice exists so a manager that is refusing for a reason a person can act on is not hidden behind `reconnecting`. It must not become a channel for copy written for a different reader: the mesh preflight's refusal ends with `run `cotal up``, which is the wrong instruction for someone whose laptop lid was shut. Aimed at cell A, where the preflight really does refuse for several backoff rungs, so a kill shows the silent branch is travelled by the real binary rather than only by cell F's hand-built input.

mutations.name: a local publish is treated as delivery, so a close frame that never left is recorded as handed back
mutations.expectRed: ...saying the manager is still holding the session, because the close frame's flush never returned
mutations.cell: ...saying the manager is still holding the session, because the close frame's flush never returned
mutations.note: Publishing is a local buffer write; the FLUSH is the round trip that says the frame left. This mutation restores the shape the code had before review: a link dying between the closed-check and the frame looked like a successful hand-back, the record was dropped, and nothing ever told the manager. It is aimed at cell I, the only cell that reaches this line with a link that is UP: a severed socket closes the connection, so the guarded branch is skipped entirely and this mutation is unreachable from every other cell. It SURVIVED against the severed cells, which is how the coverage gap was found and why the HOLD state exists.

mutations.name: the exit warns about a held session even when the seat is the thing that is gone
mutations.expectRed: held: a seat that is GONE took its own sessions with it, so there is nothing to warn about
mutations.cell: held: a seat that is GONE took its own sessions with it, so there is nothing to warn about
mutations.note: The `gone` verdict only exists because the manager answered `not-found`, and it only answers that once the seat has been freed; freeing a seat ends every session bound to it. So the sessions this line would name are already collected and naming them invents work. Aimed at the hand-built cell because the harness cannot produce the state that reaches it end to end: it needs a hand-back that FAILED on the same attempt whose control ask SUCCEEDED, over the same broker. Its sibling is mutation 8, which drives the same function's printing branch through the real binary.

mutations.name: the link deadline is unref'd again, so the timer cannot hold the process open while a dead socket is waited on
mutations.find: const deadline = new Promise<boolean>((r) => { timer = setTimeout(() => r(false), ms); });
mutations.replace: const deadline = new Promise<boolean>((r) => { const t = setTimeout(() => r(false), ms); t.unref?.(); timer = t; });
mutations.expectRed: ...exiting clean, rather than aborting on a wait that could not be bounded
mutations.cell: ...exiting clean, rather than aborting on a wait that could not be bounded
mutations.note: A wait bounded by an unref'd timer is not bounded. With something else holding the event loop open, which is true of every severed-link cell, the deadline fires and the bound looks real. On a HELD link the socket is idle, so an unref'd timer lets node empty its loop and abort the command on a pending await: exit 13, no message, the session dropped silently. Aimed at cell I, which is the only state where nothing else keeps the process alive.

mutations.name: an exit does not try the hand-back, so a detach on a link that CAME BACK still abandons the session
mutations.expectRed: ...saying NOTHING about a held session, because it handed the session back on the way out
mutations.cell: ...saying NOTHING about a held session, because it handed the session back on the way out
mutations.note: The loop released before claiming the next session, which covers every exit that stays IN the loop and none that leaves it. An operator who detaches during the backoff is the ordinary case: the link may be back, one dial would free the slot, and returning straight out leaves it held and then reports that as though nothing could be done. Aimed at cell J, which heals the link and detaches during the 30s rung so the exit path, not a reconnect, is what has to do the freeing.

mutations.name: the backoff timer is abandoned rather than cleared, so a detach holds the shell to the end of the rung
mutations.find:
const detached = watch ? await Promise.race([waited, watch.pressed.then(() => true)]) : await waited;
      clearTimeout(timer);
mutations.replace: const detached = watch ? await Promise.race([waited, watch.pressed.then(() => true)]) : await waited;
mutations.expectRed: ...and it gives the shell back on the press, not when the rung it was waiting on expires
mutations.cell: ...and it gives the shell back on the press, not when the rung it was waiting on expires
mutations.note: Losing a Promise.race does not stop a setTimeout. Without the clear, the detach is honoured at once and the terminal comes back, and then node keeps the process alive until the abandoned timer fires: measured at 27.0s with the next attempt 26.9s away and 8.3s with it 8.1s away, tracking the rung rather than any work. Aimed at cell J, which bounds the exit against where the next attempt actually falls rather than against a constant, because a constant loose enough for a slow runner is also loose enough for this.
